excerpt: What a personal injury demand letter contains, when your attorney sends one, and how insurers typically respond to it.
keyTakeaways: A personal injury demand letter is a formal document your attorney sends to the insurance company outlining liability, itemizing damages, and demanding compensation. Send after reaching MMI but before the statute of limitations expires (2 years GA, 3 years SC). Georgia's bad faith statute (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6) requires a 60-day pre-suit demand. South Carolina has no mandatory pre-suit demand for bad faith.

faqs.question: What is a personal injury demand letter?
faqs.answer: A demand letter is a formal document sent by your attorney to the at-fault party's insurance company. It outlines the facts of the accident, establishes liability, itemizes your damages, and demands a specific amount of compensation.

faqs.question: When should a demand letter be sent?
faqs.answer: After you reach maximum medical improvement (MMI). Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and South Carolina's 3-year deadline (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) set the outer boundaries.

faqs.question: What should be included in a demand letter?
faqs.answer: A factual narrative, liability argument, itemized economic damages, non-economic damages description, supporting evidence, a specific dollar demand, and a response deadline.

faqs.question: Does Georgia require a demand letter before filing a lawsuit?
faqs.answer: For standard PI claims, no. But Georgia's bad faith statute (O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6) requires a 60-day demand letter before seeking bad faith penalties. Government claims require ante litem notice — six months for a city under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5, and 12 months for a county (§ 36-11-1) or the state (§ 50-21-26).

faqs.question: What happens after the insurance company receives the demand?
faqs.answer: The insurer will accept (rare), counteroffer (most common), reject, or ignore the demand. If negotiations stall, your attorney can file a lawsuit.

faqs.question: Can I write my own demand letter?
faqs.answer: You can, but it is not recommended. A poorly drafted demand that undervalues your claim or admits fault can permanently damage your recovery. An experienced attorney maximizes the demand and anticipates insurer tactics.
